notes.meaning: Jacob continued on his journey toward the eastern lands of Mesopotamia. The Hebrew text says he lifted up his feet, showing he walked with new energy and joy after meeting God at Bethel. God's promise of protection filled him with hope for the road ahead.

Near Haran, Jacob saw a well in an open field where three flocks of sheep were resting. A large stone covered the mouth of the well to keep the water clean and prevent it from drying up. God guided Jacob directly to the place where he would find his relatives.

The local shepherds followed a rule of gathering all the flocks before rolling the heavy stone away to water the sheep. Afterward, they would put the stone back in its place. This custom made sure that everyone shared the water fairly and protected the well from sand.

Jacob greeted the waiting shepherds kindly, calling them brothers even though they were strangers. When he asked where they were from, they told him they lived in Haran. Jacob realized he had safely arrived at his mother's ancestral homeland.
Jacob asked the shepherds if they knew Laban, the grandson of Nahor. They replied that they knew him well. This direct answer showed how God was guiding Jacob's steps straight to his family.

Jacob asked whether Laban was well and in peace. The shepherds answered that he was doing well, and pointed out that Laban's daughter Rachel was arriving with the sheep. God's timing brought her to the well at that exact moment.

Jacob noticed that it was still broad daylight and too early to fold the sheep for the night. He suggested that the shepherds water the animals quickly and take them back to pasture. As a skilled shepherd himself, he encouraged them not to waste good grazing time.

The shepherds answered that they could not water their animals yet. They had an agreement to wait until all the flocks had arrived and the stone was rolled away together. They respected the community rule rather than acting alone.

While Jacob was still speaking with the men, Rachel arrived with her father's sheep. She served as a shepherdess, which was an honorable and normal task for young women in pastoral tribes. Her hard work showed her humble and responsible character.

When Jacob saw his cousin Rachel and his uncle's sheep, he stepped forward and rolled the large stone away by himself. He then drew water to take care of his uncle's flock. His bold action showed his great strength and his eagerness to serve his family.

Jacob greeted Rachel with a family kiss and wept aloud with tears of joy. He was deeply moved that God had brought him safely through the long journey to his own kin. This emotional moment marked the start of his deep love for Rachel.

Jacob explained to Rachel that he was Rebekah's son and her father's close relative. As soon as she heard this exciting news, she ran home to tell Laban. Just like her aunt Rebekah years before, she hurried to share the news of arriving family.

When Laban heard that his sister's son had arrived, he ran to meet Jacob and embraced him warmly. He brought Jacob into his house and listened as Jacob explained all that had happened. Laban welcomed him with great hospitality as family.

Laban affirmed that Jacob was truly his own flesh and blood. Jacob then stayed with him for a whole month, helping out with the work of the household. His willingness to work showed his honesty and diligence while being a guest.

Laban told Jacob that family ties were no reason for him to work without pay. He asked Jacob to name what his wages should be. Laban realized that Jacob was a valuable worker and wanted to secure his labor for the future.

The story introduces Laban's two daughters, the older named Leah and the younger named Rachel. Their names and birth order become central to everything that follows. God would use both sisters to build the families of Israel.

Leah had weak or delicate eyes, while Rachel was shapely and beautiful in face and form. In that culture, bright and lively eyes were prized, so Leah was seen as less attractive. Jacob's heart was quickly drawn to Rachel's beauty.

Because Jacob loved Rachel, he offered to work seven years for Laban in order to marry her. Jacob had no money or gifts for a traditional bride price, so he offered his personal labor instead. Seven years of work was a very large price that showed the strength of his love.

Laban accepted the offer, saying it was better to give Rachel to a relative than to a stranger. He told Jacob to stay and work with him. His response sounded agreeable, though Laban would later reveal his greedy motives.
Jacob served Laban for seven years to win Rachel. Because of his great love for her, that long period of hard labor seemed like only a few days. Deep love gave him patience and joy in his daily work.

When the seven years were finished, Jacob asked Laban for his bride so their marriage could begin. Jacob had kept his promise completely and now claimed what was fair. He trusted that Laban would honor the agreement with the same honesty.

Laban invited all the local men of the place and held a large wedding feast. In ancient times, marriage feasts brought the whole community together to witness the wedding. The public celebration made the marriage official and binding.

When night came, Laban secretly brought Leah to Jacob instead of Rachel. Because the bride wore a thick veil and the room was dark, Jacob did not realize he was with Leah. Laban used ancient wedding customs to carry out a cruel deception.

Laban gave his servant girl Zilpah to Leah to be her personal maidservant. A servant given in this way belonged entirely to the daughter, not to her husband. Zilpah would later play an important part in the growth of Jacob's family.

When morning light came, Jacob discovered that he was married to Leah. He confronted Laban angrily, asking why he had broken his promise after seven years of hard work. Jacob, who had once deceived his own father, now felt the painful sting of being deceived himself.

Laban defended himself by claiming that local custom forbade marrying off the younger daughter before the firstborn. Yet Laban had hidden this custom from Jacob for seven full years. He used local tradition as an excuse to cover up his selfish greed.

Laban told Jacob to finish the seven-day wedding celebration for Leah. In exchange for another seven years of work, Laban promised to give him Rachel as well. Laban exploited Jacob's love to extract another seven years of unpaid labor.

Jacob agreed to Laban's offer, finished the wedding week for Leah, and received Rachel as his wife too. He was willing to endure seven more years of hard work for the woman he loved. Through this complicated family, God continued His plan to build the tribes of Israel.

differ.view: Commentators note that while marrying two sisters caused family conflict, it was not yet forbidden by written law in Jacob's day and should not be labeled incest.

notes.meaning: Laban gave his servant girl Bilhah to Rachel to be her personal maidservant. Like Zilpah, Bilhah was under the direct authority of her mistress. Both of these servants would eventually bear sons who became part of Israel's twelve tribes.

Jacob was united with Rachel as his wife, and his love for her was far greater than his love for Leah. He then served Laban for an additional seven years as agreed. This favoritism between the sisters brought ongoing jealousy and sorrow into the home.

The Lord saw that Leah was unloved and showed her mercy by enabling her to have children, while Rachel was barren. In the language of Scripture, being hated often means being loved less in comparison to another. God showed special tenderness to Leah in her painful rejection.

differ.view: The word 'hated' is simply a figure of speech meaning loved less, and it should never be used to argue that God chooses to condemn certain people before birth.
Calling Leah 'hated' shows that Jacob failed in his husbandly duty, and God sovereignly stepped in to discipline Jacob and comfort the despised wife.

notes.meaning: Leah gave birth to a son and named him Reuben, which sounds like the words for seeing misery. She recognized that the Lord had seen her sorrow and hoped that her husband would now love her. Even in her deep loneliness, she looked to God for comfort.

Leah conceived again and had a second son, naming him Simeon, which means hearing. She chose this name because the Lord heard that she was unloved. Although her husband's heart had not changed, she knew God was listening to her cries.

Leah gave birth to a third son and named him Levi, which means joined or attached. She hoped that bearing three sons would finally bind Jacob's heart to her in affection. From Levi's line would later come the priests and ministers of Israel.

Leah gave birth to a fourth son and said that this time she would simply praise the Lord, naming him Judah, which means praise. She shifted her attention away from trying to earn her husband's love to thanking God. From Judah's line would later come the royal kings and the Savior.
